1446.dq: Most unaffixed words consist of one or two syllables. The stress on a two syllable word generally falls on the first syllable. ... The weight of a syllable may also affect the stress on a word.
1446.dloc: sec. 2.4 Stress, pp. 17-19 (of the SIL reapdata, the Internet Archive 20231208140355)
1446.heavy: Stated in terms of LIGHT syllables: 'The lightest of syllables are those with the short vowel, [ɨ]' (stress moves off an initial [ɨ] syllable to the next); '[ɪ], also very light' (equal stress on first two). All other vowels count as non-light. Closed syllables are explicitly NOT stress-attracting: 'If the first syllable is CV, it receives stress even if followed by CVC or CCVC.' Additional onset conditions: onsetless initial V gives equal stress, and a following syllable with a cluster/affricate onset takes the stress.
1446.dflt: initial syllable in disyllables (generally); equal stress on the first two syllables in trisyllables (generally)
1446.prule: Disyllables: stress generally on the first syllable; 'usually equal stress' on both syllables when they share the same vowel. Light initial syllable (short vowel [ɨ]) -> stress on the second syllable; initial [ɪ] (also very light) -> equal stress on first two. Onsetless initial V -> equal stress on first two, unless the second syllable begins with a consonant sequence/affricate, in which case the second syllable is stressed. Initial CV keeps stress even before CVC/CCVC (codas do not attract stress). Trisyllables: first two syllables generally receive equal stress. Partial reduplication: only first syllable stressed; complete reduplication: same syllables stressed in both halves, weaker in second half.
1446.srule: Only in complete reduplication: the copy is stressed on the same syllable as the base but more weakly ('In cases of complete reduplication the stress is on the same syllables of both halves, however it is weaker on the second half'; (65) [ˌᵐbɨ.ˈtsʲɛp ᵐbɨ.ˌtsʲɛp] 'always'). No secondary stress is described for unreduplicated words; the 'equal stress' cases in sec. 2.4 are two equal primary-marked stresses within the first two syllables, not primary plus secondary.

morph.elicq: Preface p.viii: 'The corpus for the phonological analysis, comprising some 2000 words, was collected during our stays in the village of Sepmbong between December 1981 and January 1986 and the village of Bambu in 1988.' morph.stmt: 'Verbs are words which consist of a stem that occurs with affixes indicating tense, aspect, mood, person/number of subject and object, same/different subject, and temporal linking' (p.39); all of these are suffixes except object person/number, since 'Class I verb stems all take portmanteau prefixes agreeing with the object in person and number' and class II stems 'take prefixes agreeing in number with the object: singular aŋ- or plural paŋ-' (pp.40-41) — nouns carry possessor suffixes and NP-final case/deictic enclitics, so Nankina is predominantly suffixing with a single object-prefix slot.

tn.quote: Accent in Natchez is based on pitch rather than stress. Accent falls predictably on the penultimate syllable if it contains a long vowel, otherwise on the ante-penultimate. 1449.heavy: Long vowels (two moras: /i e æ u o ɑ/) vs short vowels (one mora: /ɨ ʌ/); codas, including diphthong offglides, contribute a mora; final mora extrametrical, so a final syllable attracts stress only with long vowel + coda; a penult is heavy with a long vowel or when closed by a phonemic geminate (predictable gemination of voiceless stops does not count).
1449.dflt: antepenult (12c), e.g. úwʌda 'my burden'; disyllables without final long V + coda: initial (12b, (20)), e.g. řídɑ 'awaken', [déři] /dʌři/ 'funny'
1449.prule: Weight-sensitive three-syllable right window: stress the final syllable if it has a long vowel plus coda; else the penult if it has a long vowel (or is closed by a phonemic geminate); else the antepenult. Formalized as final-mora extrametricality + one moraic trochee at the right edge. 'Long' vowels = /i e ae u o a/ (six), 'short' (stress-repelling) = /ɨ ʌ/ (two); codas and diphthong offglides are moraic.
1449.srule: Not described. Blumenfeld 2022 states no secondary-stress rule ((20) builds a single moraic trochee at the right edge); reduplicated words carry one stress per reduplicant, and 'I am not aware of clear evidence to distinguish the two stresses in these forms as primary versus secondary' (sect. 4.6, p. 672). Hughes 2020:141: 'Within each prosodic word there is one syllable that carries primary stress'; no secondary stress described.

1454.tone: Jones (1911) identifies no lexical tone and states the stress rule separately (par. 23), but he does describe pitch, as sentence intonation: par. 27 (p. 12) 'It may be of interest to mention that the intonation of the language is somewhat different from that which we are accustomed to in Europe. The following is Mr. Nkomo's intonation of the first few sentences recorded by means of an approximate musical notation.'; par. 28 (p. 13) 'A notable feature of the Chindau intonation is the frequent use of level or very slightly rising intonation at the ends of sentences. The lowest part of the voice hardly ever seems to be used, the language affording in this... a striking contrast to the European languages.' No word-level tone contrasts are reported. Caveat (no modern source; A, B and C each and found no open Ndau phonology): Ndau is a Shona-group language (Guthrie S.10 group, Ndau S.15) and the group is standardly described as lexically tonal with penultimate prominence/lengthening; a modern primary (Mkanganwi 1973 MPhil SOAS; Mutonga 2017 PhD UZ 'The Segmental Phonology of Ndau') was not reachable, so a stricter reading could later move this record toward tone or pitch accent with penult prominence.

1457.caution: The co-cited Glennon & Glennon 2009 OPD (p. 3, 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)') says only: 'Stress is on the last syllable.' Read as a statement about surface (isolation) forms, this is consistent with Glennon 2014 (pp. 8-11): penult-stressed words drop their unstressed stem-final vowel by apocope 'when the word is spoken either in isolation or utterance-final' ([tɑ.ˈbil] < /taˈbila/, [mɑ.ˈnɑs] < /maˈnasa/, [mɑt] < /ˈmate/), so isolation forms of both classes carry stress on their last pronounced syllable; the penult-vs-final contrast holds of the phonemic vowel-final forms (OPD p. 3: 'Words that end in consonant phonetically have an underlying stem-final vowel').

1457.prule: Word stress (on the phonemic, vowel-final form) is predominantly penultimate; an open, unquantified class of words ('some words') carries phonemically (lexically) assigned final stress, exemplified by /ingˈgo/ 'I', /ingˈga/ 2SG, /giˈne/ 'here', /kaˈle/ 'get', /hiˈre/ 'tell', /liˈuo/ 'morning' vs penult /ˈmate/ 'die', /taˈbila/ 'sit', /ˈbanga/ 'see'. The contrast is diagnosable by apocope: penult-stressed words drop the unstressed stem-final vowel in isolation/utterance-finally and before vowels ([tɑ.ˈbil] < /taˈbila/, [mɑt] < /ˈmate/), final-stressed words never do ([kɑ.ˈlɛ], [hi.ˈrɛ]); no rule predicts class membership (examples span pronouns, a deictic, verbs, a noun).

1459.prule: Basic pattern (nouns, adjectives, standard prefixing verbs): stress the word-initial syllable; if the initial syllable(s) have light nuclei (/ɪ/ or epenthetic [ɪ ə]) and a full-vowel syllable follows, stress the first full-vowel syllable (leftmost heavy, else initial; attraction only rightwards). Murillo Miranda 2008 (Letras 43, p.81) reports Kopesec & Kopesec 1974 posit two suprasegmental phonemes (acento y nasalización) and that Abarca 1985 'propone que la lengua manifiesta tono alto y tono bajo' -- Abarca González 1985 (§6.3, p.35), whose main informant was the same Costa Rican speaker (Rafael Bejarano Palacios of Villa Palacios), reanalyses guaymí movere as a tonal language: 'En mi análisis por el contrario, se considera al guaymí movere como una lengua tonal.'

tn.quote: El ngäbere demuestra evidencia de lo que podrían ser vestigios de una lengua tonal. De acuerdo con el informante, hay ocasiones en que parecen haber dos tonos distintos, como por ejemplo en el caso de la primera sílaba de los siguientes ejemplos: (26.) [ŋɪ².rí¹] 'carne' [ŋí¹.rE²] 'caliente' donde '1' indica un tono más alto que '2'. Sin embargo, esta distinción siempre acompaña una diferencia constante de acento, o sea, de acuerdo con la regla a continuación: (27.) ... de manera que no se considera que la diferencia sea fonológica.
tn.translation: Ngäbere shows evidence of what could be vestiges of a tonal language. According to the informant, there are occasions on which there seem to be two distinct tones, as for example on the first syllable of the following examples: (26) [ŋɪ².rí¹] 'meat', [ŋí¹.rE²] 'hot', where '1' indicates a higher tone than '2'. However, this distinction always accompanies a constant difference of accent, that is, according to the following rule: (27) ... so that the difference is not considered to be phonological.
tn.cite: Lininger Ross, Barbara. 1981. Estudios sobre el guaymí ngäbere: fonología, alfabeto y diccionario provisional. Revista de Filología y Lingüística de la Universidad de Costa Rica 7(1-2): 101-115.
tn.note: No contrastive tone in Lininger's analysis: two phonetic pitch levels follow accent (higher = accented), called possible 'vestiges of a tonal language'. Abarca 1985 reanalyses it as H/L tonal.

1461.cfw: Lininger Ross 1981 records one unpredictable primary accent per word in Costa Rican Ngäbere (kebé 'shrimp' vs kébe 'termite'), but Abarca González 1985 analyses the same Costa Rican variety as a two-level register tone language with monosyllabic minimal pairs (kei 'tree' vs kéi 'big') and words bearing two high tones, and no later study read (Krohn 2019, Vega Chavarría 2021) settles whether the system is accent or tone.

1462.tone: Shingazidja also has a 'privative' tone system (/H/ vs zero, no phonemic L) with lexical underlying H tones, unbounded rightward tone shift within the Phonological Phrase, OCP deletion of even-numbered tones, IP-final extraprosodicity, downstep, boundary tones L%/H%, and a default H* inserted on toneless Phonological Phrases; Patin 2016:318 says the language 'exhibits characteristics of both a tone language (e.g. the shift of the tone) and a pitch-accent language' and (p.299) 'is evolving towards a pitch-accent system'. Earlier literature frames the same facts as accent (Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1989 'Nominal Accent', 1992 'Metrical Structure'; Philippson 1988, 2005 'Pitch accent in Comorian'; Jouannet 1989); Patin fn.7: 'Philippson uses the term accent for what is here referred to as tone'. Stress (penult, cued by length/intensity) is described by Patin as a separate parameter from tone.

tn.quote: Shingazidja has a ‘privative’ tone system in the sense of Hyman (2001), where /H/ contrasts with Ø (there is no phonemic low tone in Shingazidja). In this language, a high tone shifts to its right, unless an underlying tone blocks it … The shift of the tone leads to the deletion of every even-numbered underlying tone (e.g. the second tone, the fourth, the sixth, etc.), following the Obligatory Contour Principle. … stress falls regularly on the penult of words. … all high tones are downstepped with respect to the preceding high tone(s)
tn.cite: Patin, Cédric (2016). Tone and intonation in Shingazidja. In Laura J. Downing & Annie Rialland (eds.), Intonation in African Tone Languages (Phonology and Phonetics 24), 285-320. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. DOI 10.1515/9783110503524-009.

tn.note: Privative system: lexical high vs toneless, no phonemic low; H shifts rightward within the phonological phrase; downstep between highs; default H* on toneless phrases; separate regular penult stress. tn.quote: The basic tone-bearing unit in Nigerian Pidgin is the syllable (more specifically, a vowel or a syllabic sonorant). Underlyingly, syllables may bear a high tone, a low tone or no tone at all. High tone has two allotones: (a) a spreading falling tone or high-low sequence which is borne by stressed syllables: and (b) a level high tone which occurs in all other environments. ... The analysis presented in this work accounts for all of the phenomena observed by Obilade with only two basic tones, each with an unstressed level allotone and a stressed contour allotone.

1471.dq: La vocal acentuada se pronuncia con un tono bastante mas alto que las demas vocales de la palabra.
1471.dloc: Notas gramaticales pp. 68-70, 'APENDICE: EL ACENTO TONAL'
1471.prule: Lexical pitch accent ('acento tonal'): noun roots generally carry high tone on one vowel OR carry no accent at all ('Las raices sustantivales, por lo general, llevan acento en una de las vocales... o no llevan acento'; accentless roots listed: contsaro, choco, chari, sana, caniri, sibitsa, pomoro 'especie de paloma grande', tsomiri 'paujil grande'); a few trisyllabic roots carry two or three accents (mábesí, pomóró, sómámó) and disyllabic noun stems never accent both syllables. Presence and placement of accent are lexically specified: the source prints three pairs that 'difieren solamente por el acento tonal' (yógacaro 'él lo tomó' / yogacaro 'él lo guardó'; pomoro 'paloma grande' / pomóró 'caracol grande'; pë́ró 'luciérnaga' / përó 'siempre'), and in at least the first two the contrast is presence/number of accents, not position. Accent is realized by high pitch, explicitly NOT by intensity or duration. Morphology perturbs placement: possessive -te and verbal -ni tend to accent the preceding syllable (with stated exceptions), some suffixes carry their own accent, plural -ig is accented and spreads accent to all following syllables.
1471.quote: Se puede decir que el nomatsiguenga posee acento tonal, es decir que las palabras pueden tener ciertas vocales marcadas con un acento. La vocal acentuada se pronuncia con un tono bastante mas alto que las demas vocales de la palabra. La vocal acentuada no es siempre mas larga ni mas fuerte que las demas que aparecen en la palabra; en efecto, las vocales no acentuadas pueden pronunciarse con más fuerza (o mas intensidad) que la vocal acentuada. ... Puesto que la vocal acentuada se distingue principalmente por el tono alto, y no por la intensidad (mayor fuerza de la voz) o por la duracion, resu…

1471.exq_: Sin embargo, esta tendencia de acentuar la silaba que precede al sufijo posesivo -te no se cumple en todas las palabras. ... 4. Algunas combinaciones de raices y afijos crean otras excepciones a las normas generales de acentuación presentadas en este apéndice.
1471.tone: Source explicitly classifies the system as pitch accent ('acento tonal') rather than stress ('acento prosodico') or tone proper: the accented vowel is marked by high pitch only and unaccented vowels may be louder than the accented one; accent is non-obligatory (accentless noun roots are listed) and may occur two or three times in a trisyllabic root, i.e. neither obligatory nor culminative, so not a stress system; the restricted distribution (disyllabic stems never H on both syllables, no trisyllabic root with H on just the first two) is the author's argument against calling it plain 'tono'. No stress rule of any kind is given. Michael 2008 (Nanti dissertation, local cache) cites Shaver 1996: Nomatsigenga is 'apparently the only Kampan language to display contrastive tone'.

1471.cfw: Shaver 1996 (a dictionary appendix credited largely to David Payne) describes the accented vowel as marked by high pitch rather than length or loudness, but Apolinario 2020, the only acoustic study (72 nouns, six speakers), finds a duration-cued stress confined to the first two syllables of the noun (penultimate by default) with the lexical high tone a separate, non-obligatory system and states outright that Nomatsigenga is not a pitch-accent language, while Lawrence 2013, known only through Apolinario's summary, also separates tone from stress yet places the stress on the final syllable of disyllables, so both the type of system and the position of the accent remain contested among the three descriptions.

1472.dloc: Trager 1946 p.189 sec. 2:221 'Stress' (phonemic stress, no placement rule, minimal pairs); p.190 sec. 2:223 'Accentual patterns' (loud stress on any syllable of 3-4 syllable words; not further back than 4th from end); p.188 sec. 2:212 'The word' (one loud stress per word); p.198 sec. 2:32 'Accentual morphophonemics'. 1472.prule: Stress is phonemic (lexical), not positional (Trager 1946 p.189): three stress degrees loud/medial/weak (= primary/secondary/unstressed), every phonemic word has exactly one loud stress, and 'no rules on a phonemic level can be devised determining the place of the stressed syllables in a word'; minimal pairs by loud-stress position alone exist (?oh'u 'you sg. killed him': ?'ohu 'he is washing it'); nouns shift stress between singular and plural absolute forms. Two-syllable words occur with loud stress on either syllable, three- and four-syllable words on any syllable; only hedged limit: in words of more than four syllables loud stress 'do[es] not seem' to fall further back than the fourth syllable from the end (p.190). No syllable-count or weight rule.
1472.srule: Secondary stress = Trager's 'medial' stress (glossed by him as the 'secondary' stress): phonemically distinct from loud (primary) stress and lexically placed -- it occurs only in words that have a loud stress, on any number of the other syllables and in any position relative to the loud stress (p.188 sec. 2:212, p.189 sec. 2:221). Tendencies only (p.190 sec. 2:223): the syllable before the loud stress is medial or weak; if weak, the syllable before that most often has medial stress; a third syllable before the loud stress may be medial, the two following it then usually weak. In compounds the loud stresses of non-final stems are demoted to medial (p.198 sec. 2:32). Trager 1948 (IJAL 14: 157-158, secs 2.3-2.4) restates 'a number (from one up) of weak stresses or medial stresses' per word and withdraws the 1946 loud/medial complementarity in high/low-toned syllables.
1472.quote: [Trager 1946 p.189, sec. 2:221] Stress is a phonemic feature of Taos, existing in the form of loud stress, medial stress, and weak stress. 1472.tone: Trager 1946 p.189-190 sec. 2:222-2:223: threefold tone distinction (high, normal[=mid], low) only in loud- and medial-stressed syllables; normal 'by far the most common', low 'fairly common in stems', high 'limited to a few stems and suffixes'; many pairs distinguished by tone alone (c!u 'to pass by': cu[low] 'to suck'); weak-stressed syllables carry only normal tone; 'The stress system takes priority over the tone system, as is shown by the lack of tone distinctions with one of its types (weak stress), and by the fact that the word is definable in terms of the stress of syllables and not of their tone.' Hull 1973 (three tones high/falling/low, stress independent) and Sutton 2014 p.407-408 ('almost all words end up with a high or falling tone, indicating some kind of pitch accent system') as in A; tone or pitch accent remains a defensible alternative under the Hull/Sutton reanalysis, but the only full primary description (Trager) treats stress as the primary, lexically placed prosodeme.

morph.stmt: Trager 1946 §3:11 p.201: 'Taos employs the processes of affixation (prefixation, suffixation), stem-compounding, internal (morphophonemic) change, reduplication, and suppletion. Prefixation is used to express categories... of pronominal reference, status, and resolution. Suffixation is used for number, gender, dependence, tense-aspect, mode, voice. Stem-compounding is used for the expression of referential dependence [object incorporation].' — i.e. person/possessor indexing, negation, narrative/definite/interrogative status are prefixal; number-gender, TAM, subordination, voice and nominalisation are suffixal; running text shows the two sides roughly balanced…

1472.sec_quote: [p.189] Loud and medial stress are phonemically distinct, though there is some mechanical distribution of medial stress (as the "secondary" stress, the loud stress being primary) with normal tone ... [p.190] The syllable preceding loud stress may have a medial stress or a weak stress; if it is weak-stressed, then the syllable before it most often has medial stress, usually with normal tone.

tn.quote: §2:222. Tone. There is a threefold distinction of tone in Taos loud- and medial-stressed syllables, the combinations of stress and tone being phonemically distinct. The tones are high, normal, low. The normal is by far the most common, low tone is fairly common in stems, and high tone is limited to a few stems and suffixes ... There are many pairs of words distinguished by tone alone: cˈų "to pass by": cų̀ "to suck," ... In weak-stressed syllables there is only one kind of tone, which is taken to be the normal ... The stress and tone types described constitute two separate accentual systems
tn.cite: Trager, George L. 1946. An outline of Taos grammar. In Harry Hoijer et al., Linguistic Structures of Native America (Viking Fund Publications in Anthropology 6), 184-221. New York: Viking Fund.
tn.note: Three level tones (high, normal=mid, low), contrastive only in loud- and medial-stressed syllables; weak-stressed syllables normal only; phonemic stress is a separate system, 'takes priority'.
